_doc: Season definitions (Indian-context, simplified Ritucharya; user can override) and environmental influence rules. Thresholds below are transparent wellness heuristics, NOT clinical values.

Summer.diet_note: Summer (Grishma): favour cooling, hydrating foods and keep meals light.
Summer.lifestyle_note: Avoid peak-sun exposure (12–3 PM) and intense exertion in the heat.
pathya: Coconut water and cooling infusions (fennel, mint)
Juicy fruits with high water content
apathya: Very spicy, oily or fried food

Monsoon.diet_note: Monsoon (Varsha): digestion is classically weaker — favour warm, light, easily digestible food.
Monsoon.lifestyle_note: Keep dry and warm; prefer indoor activity during heavy rain.
pathya: Warm, light, easily digestible food (khichdi, moong soup)
Ginger, garlic and black pepper in cooking

Autumn.diet_note: Autumn (Sharad): favour warm, grounding, mildly astringent food as heat subsides.
Autumn.lifestyle_note: Keep regular meal times and protect against dryness.
apathya: Cold, dry and raw food in excess

Winter.diet_note: Winter (Hemanta/Shishira): digestion is classically stronger — warm, nourishing food is favoured.
Winter.lifestyle_note: Stay warm, keep a regular routine, and moisturise against dryness.
pathya: Warm nourishing one-pot meals and soups
Warm spiced drinks (turmeric milk, cinnamon tea)

Spring.diet_note: Spring (Vasanta): classically a Kapha season — favour light, dry, warming foods.
Spring.lifestyle_note: More movement and earlier mornings help counter springtime heaviness.
pathya: Barley and warm honey-water (traditional spring staples)

default.diet_note: Eat seasonally, favouring freshly cooked, easily digestible meals.

environmental_influences.explanation: Hot and dry weather is classically considered Vata-aggravating and mildly Pitta-aggravating.
Hot and humid weather is classically considered Pitta-aggravating.
High heat is classically Pitta-aggravating even without high humidity.
Cold and damp conditions are classically considered Kapha-aggravating and can disturb Vata.
Cold and dry weather is classically considered Vata-aggravating.
Rainy/monsoon conditions are classically associated with Vata and Kapha aggravation.
Moderate temperature and humidity are considered balanced conditions in classical literature.
